This disclosure describes a modular housing structure based on building information modeling (BIM) and constructed from thin-walled channel steel. The housing includes foundations, columns, beams, walls, a roof panel, doors, and windows. The columns and cross beams are made from inward-flanged C-shaped steel, or from composite square steel formed by symmetrically arranging two inward-flanged C-shaped steel members in opposite buckled engagement.

The connections between the columns and foundations, between the columns and cross beams, between neighboring cross beams, between columns or cross beams and inclined beams, between cross beams or inclined beams and the roof panel, and between adjacent support joints are achieved through base connectors, butt connectors, or cross connectors.

With the technical scheme provided in this disclosure, inward-flanged C-shaped steel members can be joined rapidly and firmly end-to-end, and composite square steel members can likewise be butt-connected quickly and reliably. Each joint includes webs and has sufficient strength to function as a standardized connector. Relief holes formed on the inner side of the joint engage with the inward flanges of the inward-flanged C-shaped steel and are pressed together, producing an internal-and-external nested connection. A positioning groove provided on the outside of the joint fits with the inward-flanged C-shaped steel in a concave-convex matching manner, after which the parts are compressed and secured by a fastening steel strip, thereby improving fastening performance and preventing slippage.

The disclosure relates to a BIM-based modular housing system constructed primarily from thin-wall channel steel. The system includes the main structural and architectural components required for a modular building, such as foundations, columns, transverse beams, walls, a roof plate, doors, and windows. By using BIM technology, the housing system can be designed, coordinated, fabricated, and assembled in a standardized and efficient manner, improving construction accuracy and reducing on-site installation time.

In the disclosed structure, the columns and transverse beams are formed using inward-flanging C-section steel. In some configurations, the structural members may also be made from combined square steel, which is produced by arranging two symmetric inward-flanging C-section steels opposite one another and buckling them together. This arrangement improves the overall rigidity and load-bearing performance of the members while retaining the lightweight advantages of thin-wall steel.

The various structural components of the modular house are connected through specially designed connectors. Depending on the installation position and connection requirement, base connectors, butting connectors, or crossed connectors may be used. These connectors are applied at key structural joints, including connections between the foundations and columns, between beams and columns, between slant beams and supporting members, between roof plates and frame members, and at other support joints throughout the building system.

The connector design allows inward-flanging C-section steel members or combined square steel members to be quickly and securely butted together. This enables rapid assembly during construction while maintaining reliable structural performance. The connectors provide strong joint engagement and improve the strength and stability of the assembled frame, making the modular housing system suitable for efficient prefabrication and on-site installation.

To further enhance the connection performance, the connectors and steel sections are provided with features such as relief holes, positioning grooves, and fastening steel strips. These features cooperate to produce nesting, fastening, and anti-slippage effects between the joints and the steel members. The relief holes facilitate proper fitting and reduce interference during assembly, the positioning grooves help align and locate the steel members accurately, and the fastening steel strips increase the clamping and locking effect. Together, these structural features improve assembly precision, prevent relative movement between connected parts, and enhance the overall safety and durability of the modular housing system.
outputs.L4:
The present disclosure relates to the technical field of building construction, and particularly to a BIM-based modular housing construction system using thin-wall channel steel. The system is suitable for rapidly assembled residential buildings, temporary buildings, light steel buildings, and other modular structures requiring standardized components, accurate installation, and reliable structural connections.

In the disclosed construction system, a building information modeling (BIM) platform is used during design, production, transportation, and on-site assembly. Through BIM modeling, the sizes, positions, quantities, connection relationships, installation sequences, and identification information of structural members are preset and coordinated. The modular housing unit may include a foundation, columns, beams, wall panels or wall frames, roof plates, doors, windows, and related connecting members. Each part can be prefabricated according to standardized dimensions and then transported to the construction site for assembly, thereby reducing on-site measurement, cutting, welding, and adjustment work.

The main load-bearing members of the modular house are preferably formed from thin-wall channel steel, especially inward-flanging C-section steel or combined square steel assembled from channel steel members. Compared with conventional heavy steel members, the thin-wall steel members have the advantages of light weight, convenient processing, easy transportation, and high installation efficiency. At the same time, by improving the connection structure between the members, the overall bearing capacity, joint strength, and stability of the assembled house can be ensured.

The system includes standardized connectors for different connection positions. These connectors may include base connectors, butting connectors, and crossed connectors. The base connectors are used for connecting vertical columns or wall frame members to a foundation or a base frame. The butting connectors are used for connecting two steel members arranged end to end, such as beams, columns, or horizontal frame members. The crossed connectors are used for connecting members intersecting with each other, for example at beam-column nodes, wall-frame intersections, roof-frame intersections, or other crossed structural positions. By standardizing these connectors, different building modules can be assembled with consistent procedures and reliable quality.

The base connector may be configured to fit within or around an inward-flanging C-section steel member. It may include a nesting portion corresponding to the inner cavity of the channel steel, a fixing portion connected to the foundation or base, and fastening holes for bolts, screws, rivets, or other fasteners. During installation, the nesting portion is inserted into the steel member or receives the steel member, so that the connector and the steel member are accurately positioned. The fastening holes are then aligned and connected using fasteners, thereby forming a stable base joint.

The butting connector may be used where two thin-wall steel members are connected in a straight line. The connector may include two oppositely arranged nesting sections respectively inserted into the ends of adjacent steel members. The nesting structure increases the contact area between the connector and the steel members and helps transfer axial force, bending moment, and shear force across the joint. The butting connector may also be provided with relief holes so that the inward flanges, folded edges, screw heads, or local protrusions of the channel steel do not interfere with insertion. This allows the connector to fit tightly with the steel member while avoiding deformation caused by forced assembly.

The crossed connector may be arranged at an intersection of two or more members. It may include receiving grooves, positioning grooves, clamping portions, or fastening strips that correspond to the shape of the C-section steel or combined square steel. The crossed connector enables intersecting members to be positioned quickly and accurately according to the BIM-generated assembly layout. After positioning, the members are fixed by bolts, self-tapping screws, rivets, clamps, or other mechanical fasteners. The crossed connector improves the integrity of wall frames, floor frames, roof frames, and beam-column joints, thereby increasing the overall stability of the modular building.

A key feature of the disclosure is that the connector system is specially adapted to inward-flanging C-section steel and combined square steel. Inward-flanging C-section steel has folded edges extending inward from the side walls of the channel, which improve the stiffness of the member but also make ordinary connection methods difficult. The disclosed connectors solve this problem through nesting structures, relief holes, positioning grooves, and fastening strips. The nesting structures allow the connector to be inserted into or matched with the hollow or semi-hollow section of the steel member. The relief holes avoid interference with inward flanges and local raised portions. The positioning grooves guide the steel member into the correct installation position and prevent misalignment. The fastening strips increase the local fastening area and improve resistance to loosening and slippage.

In some embodiments, the combined square steel is formed by joining two inward-flanging C-section steel members together to create an approximately rectangular or square section. The connectors may be designed to match the internal cavity, external contour, or flange arrangement of the combined square steel. This allows the combined square steel to be used as columns, beams, or other high-strength members in the modular housing system. Because the connector engages with multiple surfaces of the steel member, the joint can resist axial loading, bending, torsion, shear, and lateral displacement more effectively than a simple surface-fastened joint.

During construction, the BIM model may generate a component list, processing drawings, installation codes, and connection node diagrams. Each foundation member, column, beam, wall member, roof plate, door frame, window frame, and connector can be labeled according to its position in the model. At the factory, the thin-wall steel members are cut, punched, formed, and marked according to BIM data. The connectors are also manufactured with standardized holes, grooves, relief openings, and fastening portions. At the construction site, workers assemble the components according to the BIM installation sequence and corresponding component codes.

The assembly process may include fixing the base connectors to the foundation, installing columns or vertical frame members, connecting beams or horizontal members with butting and crossed connectors, assembling wall frames and wall plates, installing roof plates, and finally installing doors and windows. Since the connectors provide positioning and nesting functions, the members can be aligned quickly without repeated manual adjustment. Since most connections are completed by mechanical fastening rather than welding, construction speed is increased, weather dependence is reduced, and on-site quality is easier to control.

The disclosed connection system provides several technical advantages. First, it improves installation speed because the components are standardized and can be rapidly positioned through nesting and grooves. Second, it improves connection strength because the connector is not merely attached to the surface of the thin-wall steel, but is fitted with the shape of the steel member and transfers force through multiple contact surfaces. Third, it improves fastening reliability because fastening strips and aligned fastening holes increase the clamping area and reduce local deformation of thin-wall steel. Fourth, it improves anti-slippage performance because positioning grooves, nesting portions, and crossed connector structures restrict relative movement between members. Fifth, it improves overall building safety because the joints have better resistance to loosening, bending, torsion, and shear.

The system is also beneficial for industrialized and modular construction. By combining BIM-based design with standardized thin-wall steel connectors, the disclosed solution enables high repeatability, reduced material waste, shortened construction periods, and improved construction accuracy. It is particularly suitable for prefabricated modular housing in which structural members, wall units, roof units, door openings, and window openings must be assembled quickly while maintaining reliable structural performance.

Accordingly, the disclosure provides a BIM-based modular housing construction technology using thin-wall channel steel and a standardized connector system. The foundations, columns, beams, walls, roof plates, doors, and windows are assembled through base connectors, butting connectors, and crossed connectors. The connector system is especially suitable for inward-flanging C-section steel or combined square steel and uses nesting engagement, relief holes, positioning grooves, and fastening strips to enhance joint strength, fastening reliability, and anti-slippage performance. As a result, the modular housing structure can be assembled rapidly, securely, and with high structural strength.

## Patent Summary

The invention relates to the technical field of prefabricated buildings, in particular to a BIM-based prefabricated modular housing system using thin-wall channel steel and combined square steel formed by oppositely buckled C-section members.

The modular housing system comprises a plurality of prefabricated building modules, each of which is designed, processed, transported, and assembled based on a Building Information Modeling (BIM) platform. The BIM platform is used to establish a three-dimensional digital model of the modular house, integrate structural components, connection nodes, pipelines, openings, decoration layers, and installation information, and generate processing and assembly data for factory manufacturing and on-site installation.

The structural frame of each module is mainly composed of thin-wall channel steel members and combined square steel members. The combined square steel members are formed by oppositely buckling two C-section steel members and connecting them together to form a square or substantially rectangular closed section. The combined square steel members may be used as columns, beams, edge frames, corner posts, or reinforcing members of the modular unit, while the thin-wall channel steel members may be used as secondary beams, wall studs, roof purlins, floor joists, or connecting members. The oppositely buckled C-section members improve the overall rigidity, bearing capacity, torsional resistance, and stability of the structural frame while maintaining the advantages of light weight, convenient processing, and low material consumption.

The prefabricated modular housing system further includes wall panels, floor panels, roof panels, connecting nodes, lifting points, and reserved interfaces for electrical, water supply, drainage, ventilation, and other building services. The components are manufactured in a factory according to BIM-generated drawings and data, and the prefabricated modules are transported to a construction site for rapid assembly. Adjacent modules may be connected through bolted, welded, or combined connection structures so as to form single-story or multi-story modular buildings.

Compared with conventional prefabricated housing, the invention has the advantages of accurate digital design, reduced design conflicts, high manufacturing precision, improved assembly efficiency, reduced construction waste, shortened construction period, and enhanced structural performance. The combined square steel formed by oppositely buckled C-section members provides better load-bearing capacity and deformation resistance than a single thin-wall section, and is suitable for standardized production of modular housing units. The BIM-based design and management method enables full-process coordination from design to manufacturing, transportation, installation, operation, and maintenance, thereby improving the industrialization and informatization level of prefabricated modular housing.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the technical solution and beneficial effects of a modular building system where inward-flanging C-section steel components are connected by standardized high-strength joints with webs, relief holes, positioning grooves, and fastening steel strips.
counterfactuals.output:
The system is a modular steel building structure formed from standardized inward-flanging C-section steel members and matching high-strength connection joints. It is intended to allow wall, floor, roof, column, beam, and corner modules to be assembled quickly and accurately while maintaining high structural strength.

## Technical solution

The building system uses prefabricated C-section steel components whose flanges are turned inward. The inward flanges improve section stiffness, provide protected fastening edges, and allow adjacent components to be joined without large exposed protrusions.

At the connection positions, standardized high-strength joint members are used. Each joint is shaped to match the internal geometry of the C-section steel and may include:

1. **Web plates or reinforcing webs**  
   The joint contains one or more webs that fit into or against the web portion of the C-section member. These webs increase bearing area, improve load transfer, and prevent local deformation at the connection.

2. **Relief holes**  
   Holes or cut-outs are formed in the joint body to avoid interference with bent flanges, weld seams, bolt heads, or manufacturing tolerances. The relief holes also reduce stress concentration and can reduce component weight.

3. **Positioning grooves**  
   Grooves, slots, or recesses are provided to guide the C-section steel components into the correct installation position. These grooves ensure that the members are aligned in a fixed orientation during assembly.

4. **Fastening steel strips**  
   Steel strips are arranged along the joint or inside the C-section member to provide bolting, riveting, screwing, or welding surfaces. The strips strengthen the connection area and distribute fastening loads over a larger region.

The C-section steel components and the high-strength joints are preferably standardized in size and hole pattern. During assembly, the C-section steel members are inserted, sleeved, clamped, or overlapped with the joint, positioned by the grooves, and then secured using bolts, screws, rivets, or other fasteners through preformed holes and fastening strips.

The joints can be configured as straight joints, corner joints, T-joints, cross joints, column-beam joints, wall-frame joints, roof-frame joints, or floor-frame joints. Because the same connection principles are used throughout the building, different modules can be connected in a repeatable and interchangeable manner.

## Beneficial effects

1. **High structural strength**  
   The combination of inward-flanging C-section steel, reinforcing webs, and fastening steel strips improves bending resistance, shear resistance, and torsional stability at the joints.

2. **Reliable load transmission**  
   Loads are transferred through webs, flanges, and fastening strips rather than being concentrated at a single bolt or thin plate. This reduces local buckling, tearing, and deformation.

3. **Accurate and fast assembly**  
   Positioning grooves guide the components into place, reducing measurement errors and simplifying on-site installation. Workers can assemble modules quickly using standardized fasteners.

4. **Improved modularity**  
   Since the joints and C-section members are standardized, the same parts can be used for different building layouts. This supports industrialized production and mass customization.

5. **Reduced construction time**  
   Prefabricated steel members and predesigned joints reduce welding and cutting on site. Most assembly can be completed by bolting or mechanical fastening.

6. **Better dimensional consistency**  
   Grooves, relief holes, and matched joint geometry help control tolerances and ensure that frame members remain square, straight, and aligned.

7. **Lower material waste**  
   Standard lengths, repeated joint designs, and prefabricated connection parts reduce the need for custom cutting and rework.

8. **Convenient transportation and replacement**  
   Modular C-section members and detachable joints are easier to package, transport, assemble, disassemble, and replace compared with large welded frames.

9. **Enhanced safety and durability**  
   Stronger joint regions improve seismic resistance, wind resistance, and overall building stability. The inward flanges also protect edges and fastening locations from accidental damage.

10. **Suitable for industrialized building construction**  
   The system is well suited for prefabricated houses, modular buildings, light steel structures, temporary buildings, container-type buildings, and rapidly assembled construction projects.

## Formal Patent Language Draft

### Title  
**BIM-Based Modular Housing Structure Using Thin-Walled Channel Steel Members and Anti-Slip Interlocking Connectors**

### Abstract  
A modular housing structure designed for Building Information Modeling (BIM)-assisted prefabrication and rapid assembly is disclosed. The structure comprises a plurality of thin-walled channel steel columns, beams, slant beams, roof plates, and connection members. The connection members are configured to enable rapid and secure butting, nesting, pressing engagement, and slippage prevention between adjacent structural components. The modular housing structure allows standardized digital design, factory prefabrication, efficient transportation, and quick on-site installation while maintaining structural stability, positioning accuracy, and connection reliability.

---

### Technical Field  
The invention relates to the technical field of prefabricated buildings, and more particularly to a BIM-based modular housing structure formed by thin-walled channel steel columns, beams, slant beams, roof plates, and associated connectors for rapid assembly and secure structural connection.

---

### Background  
Conventional modular housing systems often require extensive on-site welding, bolting, measuring, and alignment, resulting in long construction periods, high labor costs, and inconsistent installation quality. Existing prefabricated structures may also suffer from inaccurate positioning of components, weak resistance to relative sliding at joints, and reduced assembly efficiency.

With the development of Building Information Modeling (BIM), modular components can be digitally designed and prefabricated with higher precision. However, there remains a need for a modular housing structure that combines BIM-based standardized component design with thin-walled channel steel members and specially configured connectors capable of quick butting, nesting, pressing, and anti-slip engagement.

---

### Summary of the Invention  
The invention provides a BIM modular housing structure comprising a structural frame formed from thin-walled channel steel columns, horizontal beams, inclined slant beams, roof plates, and a plurality of connectors. The connectors are arranged at intersections and joints of the columns, beams, slant beams, and roof plates. Each connector is configured to receive and position a corresponding channel steel member, thereby allowing adjacent components to be quickly butted and nested together.

In certain embodiments, the connectors include pressing portions, limiting portions, insertion portions, receiving grooves, flanges, ribs, or anti-slip surfaces configured to prevent relative displacement between connected components after assembly. The connector may provide a mechanical locking relationship with the thin-walled channel steel member to improve assembly accuracy and structural integrity.

The modular housing structure may be generated, coordinated, and numbered through a BIM model, such that each column, beam, slant beam, roof plate, and connector is prefabricated according to digital design data and assembled on site according to predetermined spatial positions.

---

### Detailed Description  
The BIM modular housing structure includes a plurality of vertical thin-walled channel steel columns arranged at predetermined positions to define the vertical load-bearing framework of a housing module. A plurality of horizontal thin-walled channel steel beams are connected between the columns to form floor, wall, or roof frame portions. A plurality of slant beams are connected between corresponding columns, beams, or roof portions to form an inclined support structure. Roof plates are mounted on or connected to the slant beams or upper beams to form a roof assembly.

The thin-walled channel steel members may each have a generally C-shaped, U-shaped, or channel-shaped cross section. The open channel portion of each member may be configured to cooperate with a connector, such that the connector at least partially nests within the channel, or the channel at least partially nests around the connector. This nesting relationship facilitates rapid positioning and improves joint strength.

The connectors may be disposed at column-beam joints, beam-beam joints, beam-slant beam joints, slant beam-roof plate joints, or column-roof frame joints. Each connector may include one or more of:  
1. a butting surface configured to abut an end face of a channel steel member;  
2. a nesting portion configured to enter or receive a channel portion of the channel steel member;  
3. a pressing portion configured to press against a side wall, web, or flange of the channel steel member;  
4. a limiting portion configured to restrict axial, lateral, or rotational movement; and  
5. an anti-slip portion configured to prevent relative slippage between adjacent structural members.

The anti-slip portion may comprise teeth, ribs, projections, recesses, serrations, friction-enhancing surfaces, locking tabs, bolt holes, self-locking wedges, or cooperating interlocking formations. In some embodiments, fasteners such as bolts, rivets, screws, pins, or clamps may be used together with the connector to further secure the structural members. In other embodiments, the connector may provide preliminary self-positioning or self-locking prior to final fastening.

The roof plates may be prefabricated panels configured to be supported by the slant beams or roof beams. The roof plates may include edge portions adapted to overlap, butt, nest, or interlock with adjacent roof plates or roof frame members. Connectors may be provided along roof plate edges to prevent sliding under wind load, vibration, or thermal movement.

A BIM model may be established before fabrication to define the dimensions, locations, component identifiers, connection relationships, and assembly sequence of all modular elements. The columns, beams, slant beams, roof plates, and connectors may be manufactured according to the BIM data, marked with corresponding identification codes, and transported to a construction site for rapid assembly. The BIM model may also be used to verify collision avoidance, optimize material usage, and guide installation.

---

## Example Claims

### Claim 1  
A BIM modular housing structure, comprising:  
a plurality of thin-walled channel steel columns;  
a plurality of thin-walled channel steel beams connected to the columns;  
a plurality of thin-walled channel steel slant beams connected to at least one of the columns and the beams;  
a plurality of roof plates supported by the slant beams or the beams; and  
a plurality of connectors disposed at joints between the columns, the beams, the slant beams, and the roof plates;

### Possible Independent Method Claim

### Claim 21  
A method of constructing a BIM modular housing structure, comprising:  
generating a BIM model of a modular housing structure including thin-walled channel steel columns, beams, slant beams, roof plates, and connectors;  
fabricating the columns, beams, slant beams, roof plates, and connectors according to data obtained from the BIM model;  
transporting the fabricated components to an installation site;  
connecting the columns, beams, slant beams, and roof plates by positioning the connectors at predetermined joints;  
butting and nesting the thin-walled channel steel members with the connectors;  
pressing the connectors against the thin-walled channel steel members; and  
securing the connected components such that relative slippage between the components is prevented.

### Advantages of the Invention  
The disclosed BIM modular housing structure provides at least the following advantages:

1. rapid on-site assembly through standardized prefabricated components;  
2. improved positioning accuracy through BIM-based design and connector-guided alignment;  
3. secure mechanical connection through butting, nesting, pressing, and anti-slip engagement;  
4. reduced dependence on welding and complex field operations;  
5. improved transportation and manufacturing efficiency using thin-walled channel steel members; and  
6. enhanced structural stability of modular housing units.
